Perfect
per'fekt
a. (complete, whole, entire; rendering Hebrew tamim, Greek teleios)
From the Latin perfectus, perficio, to finish through — carried to its end. Hebrew tamim means whole, sound, without blemish, and is the word for an unblemished sacrificial animal; Greek teleios is from telos, an end or goal, and means having reached its intended completion.

Biblical Definition

Perfect in the Authorized Version rarely means sinless. It means whole, complete, entire, brought to the end for which the thing was made. Job is called “perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil” (Job 1:1), and the book then spends forty chapters showing a man who is manifestly not sinless; tamim describes his integrity, the absence of a divided heart, not the absence of sin. The same word governs the sacrificial law, where a perfect lamb is an unblemished one — sound, entire, fit to be offered. Of things that come from God the word can be taken absolutely: “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psalm 19:7), lacking nothing it should contain. Of men it is a word of direction as much as of state. When our Lord says “Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect” (Matthew 5:48), the context is loving enemies, and the sense is completeness of love that does not stop at the boundary of those who love us in return — a whole love answering to a whole God. The covenant charge to Abram sets the same direction: “I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect” (Genesis 17:1), where wholeness of walk is commanded on the ground of who God is. Perfection is thus the goal toward which sanctification genuinely moves, reached not in this life but at glorification.

Webster 1828 Definition

Complete, whole, entire, without blemish — not, in most biblical usage, sinless. Job is perfect in integrity; a lamb is perfect in soundness; the law is perfect absolutely.

expand to see more

PERFECT, a. [L. perfectus, perficio, to complete; per and facio, to do.] Finished; complete; consummate; not defective; having all that is requisite to its nature and kind.

2. Fully informed; completely skilled; as, perfect in the art.

3. Complete in moral excellencies; blameless; as, a perfect heart.

4. In Scripture, upright and sincere, without a divided heart; as, Job was perfect and upright, Job 1.

5. Of a sacrifice, sound and without blemish; as, your lamb shall be perfect, Exod. 12.

Key Scripture

Job 1:1 — "There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil."

Psalm 19:7 — "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple."

Matthew 5:48 — "Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect."

Genesis 17:1 — "And when Abram was ninety years old and nine, the LORD appeared to Abram, and said unto him, I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect."

Modern Corruption

Read as sinless, the word breeds either perfectionism or despair. Read as Scripture uses it — whole, undivided, unblemished — it describes an integrity God actually works in his people now.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors grow from the same mistranslation. Wesleyan and later holiness teaching read perfect as attainable sinlessness in this life and produced a doctrine of entire sanctification that Scripture will not carry; the same Job who is called perfect abhors himself and repents in dust and ashes. Running the other way, an honest man who reads Matthew 5:48 as a demand for sinlessness concludes the command is impossible and quietly files it away. Both readings mistake wholeness for flawlessness.

There is also a flattening in modern speech, where perfect has become a courtesy noise — an answer to a confirmed appointment. A word emptied by overuse cannot bear the weight of Psalm 19:7. The principle to recover is the sacrificial sense that underlies the whole vocabulary: what is offered to God must be entire, unblemished, not the leftover or the divided. That standard condemns half-hearted worship far more searchingly than a demand for sinlessness would, and it points where the whole system points, to the one unblemished Lamb whose perfection is reckoned to those who trust him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tamim is whole and unblemished, from tamam, to be complete; it is the sacrificial standard. Greek teleios is from telos, the end or goal, and denotes a thing that has arrived at what it was for.

expand to see more

Hebrew tamim (H8549) — whole, sound, without blemish; the required quality of a sacrifice.

Hebrew tamam (H8552) — to be complete, to be finished; the verbal root behind the adjective.

Hebrew tom (H8537) — integrity, simplicity of heart; the undivided quality ascribed to Job.

Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, full-grown, having reached its telos.

Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend or fit together; the verb behind make you perfect in Hebrews 13:21.

Usage

"Of a man's undivided integrity, not his sinlessness: that man was perfect and upright (Job 1:1)."

"Of the law taken absolutely: the law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul (Psalm 19:7)."

"Of wholeness of walk commanded on the ground of who God is: walk before me, and be thou perfect (Genesis 17:1)."
